I have always loved the hour when the sun drops low enough to turn ordinary windows into sheets of copper. It is a brief, unreliable magic. In summer it stretches, syrupy and long; in winter it arrives without warning and leaves before you have found your coat.

I like to walk in that hour. The day’s arguments shrink. People move a little slower, as if the softening light has given them permission to be tired. Dogs pull less on their leashes. Cars switch on their headlights one by one, and the street becomes a string of patient, glowing animals.

Last Tuesday, I watched a man on a ladder untangle a string of lights from a tree. He was not in a hurry. Below him, a child held the ladder and stared up as if he were performing a miracle. The whole scene was washed in that amber light, and for a moment it looked like a painting that had not yet decided what it was about.

I think we are all a little more honest in the last hour of light. The outlines of things grow uncertain, and so do we. We stop performing. We remember that the day was not entirely ours, but the dusk can be. Then the streetlights blink on, and the spell breaks. We go inside, make dinner, argue over small things. But the copper windows stay with me longer than they should. They are proof that beauty does not need a reason. It only needs someone to look.

"On Keeping a List of Small Joys"

I started keeping a list of small joys on the back of a receipt. It was not an ambitious project. The first entry read: 'The sound of a train passing two streets away, low and unhurried.' The second: 'A stranger holding the door open with their elbow because their hands were full of grocery bags.' The third: 'The particular blue of a February sky at 5:42 p.m., just before the streetlights blink on.'

The list grew, not because my life became more remarkable, but because I had given myself permission to notice it. A small joy is not the same as happiness. Happiness can feel like weather—large, variable, sometimes arriving without warning. A small joy is more like a pebble you choose to put in your pocket. It has weight. You can return to it later and turn it over in your palm.

Most entries are unremarkable to anyone else. The smell of a library book opened for the first time in decades. The way my neighbor's cat sits in the exact center of the sidewalk, as if the whole street were a stage. The first sip of coffee when the mug is still too hot to hold comfortably. These things do not solve problems or change outcomes. But they remind me that attention is a form of affection. To notice the world closely is to love it a little, even when it does not love you back.

I still keep the list in a notes app now, not on receipts. But the original receipt is folded in the back of my wallet, faded at the creases. It says, in smudged ink: 'The way wet leaves stick to the windshield, like small hands letting go.' I have never once been sorry I looked.
